subtitle: Look at who can reach a grant or contract opportunity, what the proposed requirements ask and how review choices are made. Throughout, actual funding, contracting and award responsibilities stay clear.
scope: For leaders and staff across DHS who examine grants, procurement and opportunity access. Complete original example and practice calculations are not actual solicitations, organizations, ratings, awards, service results or approval authority. Use applicable current funding, contracting, conflict, accessibility and formal equity processes. Complete any required grants-management training as well; this course does not replace it. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff do their own equity work. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referral-only to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: Follow Tamsin and Galen from an information-access idea through a document-task inquiry, complete practice rubric calculations and a corrected account. Mera and Dorian’s book-exchange encounter opens a question about what an invitation communicates. Keep the particular evidence, actual responsibilities and later effects distinct. Private understanding is available without a live award, applicant record or public work product.

lessons.title: Identify the funding choice before judging the process
lessons.summary: Distinguish the purpose, proposed opportunity and applicable process before claiming who will benefit.
lessons.objective: Describe the purpose and limits of Tamsin’s practice grant idea.
objectives: Describe the purpose and limits of Tamsin’s practice grant idea.
Distinguish a grant inquiry from a procurement purchase and an approved award.
Identify one relevant process question without inventing a recipient or service result.
takeaways: A stated public purpose does not establish an approved opportunity.
Different funding arrangements need their actual requirements.
A possible access barrier is a question to examine, not a finding about an organization.
lessons.statement: Start with what is being proposed, why it matters and which decisions remain open.

image.caption: Two people review an open printed document, with one pointing to a line.

intro.heading: Identify the funding choice before judging the process
intro.body:
In an original practice DHS planning conversation, Tamsin proposes funding community learning sessions about how to find service information. Galen asks whether the idea is a grant supporting a public purpose or a purchase of a defined service for the state. The example describes an intended information-access purpose. It supplies no appropriation, actual solicitation, eligible organization, contract amount, funding condition or delegated award authority. The first useful action is to describe that boundary.

Grants and purchasing arrangements should not be treated as interchangeable simply because both involve money and a contract. The current Office of Grants Management page distinguishes support for a legally authorized public purpose from a professional/technical purchase for the state’s direct benefit. Tamsin should establish the arrangement with the responsible contracting process before borrowing a template or assuming a particular selection method. This course cannot make that determination for an actual program.

Once the purpose is clear, ask how a potential applicant would encounter the proposed opportunity. A notice may be hard to locate; a requirement may be unclear; an application method may be difficult to use. These are possible process barriers. The example contains no observation that any particular organization missed a notice or lacked capacity. An organization’s size, location or familiar name does not answer those questions.

Galen can recommend an inquiry into the proposal’s fit, information and process requirements. That recommendation is distinct from approving a solicitation, selecting a recipient or verifying a service benefit. Relevant program, financial, contracting and legal responsibilities remain with their actual processes. Consultant guidance can deepen staff understanding without taking over those decisions or creating a mandatory consultant review of every staff question.

For private practice, describe the proposed purpose in one sentence and identify one unanswered process question. You can use the example throughout. No real applicant information, live award or public account of your learning is needed. A clearer distinction is useful even when it leads to further inquiry rather than an immediate funding decision.

flashcards.back: Tamsin wants to support learning about finding service information. The purpose explains the idea; it does not establish eligibility, funding or an outcome.
Ask whether the arrangement supports the applicable authorized public purpose and grant requirements. A course example cannot supply that authority.
Ask whether the state is acquiring a defined product or service under its actual purchasing process. The name of a template does not settle the arrangement.
An actual award depends on the applicable decision and agreement process. A planning conversation is not permission to spend or begin funded work.

items.title: Describe the idea precisely
items.body: Keep the intended information-access purpose visible while stating that its amount, participants and authority are not supplied. This gives the responsible process a useful question rather than an invented complete program.

items.title: Find the applicable arrangement
items.body: A grant and a purchase have different purposes and requirements. Bring the facts of the proposed arrangement to the actual contracting responsibility instead of picking whichever template seems easiest.

items.title: Preserve the service question
items.body: Even an actual funded session would not alone show that people understood or could use service information. Identify later evidence questions without calling the proposed activity an established benefit.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretations and their implications

tabs.label: Use the nearest template
tabs.body: A familiar document can help locate questions, but copying it does not establish the arrangement or its requirements. Tamsin still needs the applicable process before treating an inherited clause as either essential or unnecessary.

tabs.label: Choose recipients first
tabs.body: A preferred organization may have valuable experience, but the example describes no eligibility or selection authority. Starting with a desired recipient can obscure the purpose and the required process.

tabs.label: Clarify purpose and process
tabs.body: Galen can retain the learning purpose and ask which actual arrangement applies. That supports further analysis while keeping funding, approval and service-result questions open.

check.question: What can Galen accurately say about the example?
check.correct: Tamsin proposes an information-access learning idea; the actual funding arrangement, authority and effects still need examination.
wrong: The proposal establishes a grant that any organization can receive.
A familiar contract template decides which arrangement applies.
The consultant can approve the funding because the purpose is equitable.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The intended purpose is supplied; the arrangement and decisions are not.
check.feedbackIncorrect: No eligibility, funding or grant determination is supplied. A template does not establish the facts or applicable arrangement. Program leadership and equity guidance do not confer contracting or fiscal authority.

sorting.heading: Keep evidence, inquiry and decisions distinct

items.text: Tamsin proposes learning sessions about finding information.
The intended purpose is information access.
Which funding arrangement applies?
What evidence would show a useful service-information effect?
Every organization is approved to receive funding.
The proposal proves service access improved.

scenario.context: Practice planning: Tamsin calls the learning idea an approved community grant. No actual arrangement or award process is supplied.
options: Choose a recipient before checking the arrangement.

Use the older template as approval.
responses: A preferred recipient cannot replace the actual purpose, eligibility and selection process.
This preserves the useful idea without inventing a grant or an award.
The inherited document does not authorize the proposed opportunity.

lessons.transfer: Privately describe the practice purpose and one actual-process question that prevents an unsupported award claim.

move.control: You can distinguish an idea from the decisions needed to act on it.
move.failure: A useful purpose becomes an invented approved opportunity.
move.next: Retain the purpose and ask which actual arrangement and responsibilities apply.

lessons.title: Trace a possible barrier without inventing its cause
lessons.summary: Follow the application task and distinguish observed difficulty, a hypothesis and the evidence still needed.
lessons.objective: Identify the task barrier in an original application-format example.
objectives: Identify the task barrier in an original application-format example.
Distinguish an organization’s comment from a general claim about all applicants.
Compare a proposed usable format with a change to substantive requirements.
takeaways: Examine the step where a person encounters difficulty.
One report does not establish the cause of every missing application.
Usable presentation can support access while actual eligibility and review remain unchanged.
lessons.statement: Follow the real task before explaining why people did or did not participate.

image.caption: Two people review an open printed document, with one pointing to a line.

intro.heading: Trace a possible barrier without inventing its cause
intro.body:
Galen examines an invented early draft containing an application-instructions page saved only as an image. During an informal practice usability inquiry, Ellis says that the image does not provide text that their reading software can follow. The example describes that particular task difficulty. It does not supply Ellis’s diagnosis, organization size, preferred language, eligibility or willingness to apply. Galen should keep the reported barrier attached to the task.

The draft’s information needs a usable structure, not a guess about Ellis. A proposed text-based version with clear headings and accurately labeled links may let a reader move through the instructions. It should preserve the actual conditions and the authoritative opportunity information. A plain summary is useful only if it does not quietly alter an eligibility requirement, omit a necessary obligation or disagree with the official instructions.

Consider a separate observation: only familiar organizations responded to a previous announcement. That is a participation pattern, not a complete explanation. The record does not say who saw the notice, who considered it, why someone declined or what resources an application required. Distribution, clarity, timing, fit and other explanations remain possible. Galen should ask about evidence before declaring that a particular factor caused the pattern.

The distinction affects the proposed repair. Rebuilding the instructional format addresses the image-only task barrier. It does not waive insurance, reporting or financial conditions, guarantee accessible use by every person, or establish that new applicants will succeed. Wider publicity addresses a different question: whether potential applicants encounter the opportunity. Any actual change to a posted document or process needs the responsible review and communication route.

The DHS content guidance supports clearer, usable information. It is not evidence that the entire imagined solicitation meets every applicable accessibility standard. For private practice, separate Ellis’s reported difficulty from an untested explanation for participation. Then describe how a proposed format change might help and what would still need checking. You can learn the distinction without collecting an organization’s private records or making a real solicitation change.

flashcards.back: Ellis reports that the image-only instructions lack text their reading software can follow. The reported interaction is evidence; a diagnosis or motive is not supplied.
A count of familiar respondents describes the observed pool. It does not identify who missed the opportunity or why another organization did not apply.
A structured text version may improve navigation while retaining the actual requirements. Its usefulness needs checking with the task, not a declaration of universal access.
Eligibility, financial and service conditions are distinct from presentation. A clearer page does not authorize staff to remove those obligations.

items.title: Keep the report specific
items.body: Record the instructional task and the difficulty Ellis described. Do not replace the account with an assumed disability, organizational capacity or preferred remedy that the case never supplied.

items.title: Compare competing explanations
items.body: Familiar-only participation could involve opportunity awareness, program fit or another factor. Ask which observation would distinguish those possibilities instead of treating a single count as a causal finding.

items.title: Check the proposed repair
items.body: A structured text version should preserve meaning and authoritative instructions. Test whether the actual reading task becomes usable, and keep other users, conditions and formal posting decisions open.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretations and their implications

tabs.label: Blame applicant capacity
tabs.body: An assumption that Ellis cannot manage a grant turns a document problem into an unsupported organization judgment. The task report says nothing about delivery or financial capacity.

tabs.label: Waive a requirement quietly
tabs.body: Removing an obligation may appear helpful, but a format complaint does not confer authority to change substantive conditions. The actual responsible review still applies.

tabs.label: Improve the format and examine reach
tabs.body: Propose a usable version for the instruction task and a separate inquiry into participation. This distinguishes mechanisms and prevents one improvement from being credited with effects it has not shown.

check.question: What does Ellis’s report establish?
check.correct: The image-only instruction task presents the reported reading-software barrier; organizational capacity and wider participation causes remain unknown.
wrong: Ellis’s organization cannot deliver the funded work.
The familiar-only response pool proves the notice was never seen by anyone else.
A text version removes all eligibility and accessibility concerns.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The reported difficulty is specific, and the broader explanations remain untested.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The report concerns a document task, not delivery capacity. The response pool does not reveal who encountered or declined the notice. A format improvement changes neither actual eligibility nor every access condition.

sorting.heading: Keep evidence, inquiry and decisions distinct

items.text: Ellis reports that image-only instructions lack readable text.
The imagined prior pool contains familiar organizations.
Could wider publicity change opportunity awareness?
Would structured text improve this reading task?
Every missing applicant lacked capacity.
One format repair proves universal access.

lessons.next: Continue to understand what an invitation communicates.

scenario.context: Practice draft: Ellis describes an image-only reading barrier. Tamsin concludes that small organizations need fewer fiscal requirements. No size or financial evidence is supplied.
options: Accept the capacity conclusion and remove requirements.
Offer only a different award to Ellis.
Separate the format report, propose a usable version and retain actual fiscal and participation questions.
responses: The task difficulty establishes neither size nor a reason to waive an actual obligation.
A task barrier does not determine award eligibility or entitlement.
This addresses the supplied barrier without inventing organizational facts or authority.

lessons.transfer: Privately state the reading task, a proposed improvement and one effect the case still does not establish.

move.control: You can keep an access observation tied to its actual task.
move.failure: One report becomes a broad capacity or participation judgment.
move.next: Compare the repair’s mechanism with the particular evidence still needed.

lessons.title: Understand what an invitation communicates
lessons.summary: Examine personally learned meanings of an offer and preserve both genuine inquiry and clear decision limits.
lessons.objective: Describe Mera’s and Dorian’s different learned meanings of an invitation.
objectives: Describe Mera’s and Dorian’s different learned meanings of an invitation.
Identify how an apparently welcoming phrase can imply a decision not yet made.
Revise the invitation so open influence and retained responsibility are clear.
takeaways: A familiar phrase can carry different meanings for different people.
Clarifying a boundary can preserve participation rather than close it.
An inquiry must have real room for influence without promising a selection.
lessons.statement: Ask what the invitation means to its receiver before calling it clear or welcoming.

image.caption: Two people review an open printed document, with one pointing to a line.

intro.heading: Understand what an invitation communicates
intro.body:
In a separate example, Mera and Dorian plan a neighborhood book exchange. Mera grew up helping prepare family gatherings where an invitation to bring a display meant that a place had been held for the guest. Keeping that commitment expressed dependable welcome. Dorian learned from a community garden exchange where an invitation to discuss a display meant an open idea that the organizers would consider alongside others. Being invited into that discussion expressed shared exploration, not a reserved place.

Dorian says, “We’d like to invite you to explore a display.” Mera hears a place promised and begins preparing one. Dorian hears an invitation to shape a possible idea and has not reserved a place. Neither account establishes a national, ethnic, religious or generational rule. These are personally learned meanings supplied for two people in the example in this particular encounter. Their different interpretations matter because preparation and responsibility follow from them.

They can clarify the invitation without judging either person. Dorian can explain that display choices are open, identify what Mera can influence and retain the organizer’s responsibility for selection. Mera can explain that the phrase sounded like a commitment. An invitation that asks for ideas should offer actual room to change the design, not solicit effort after the decision is already settled. Clear boundaries and meaningful participation can exist together.

Return to Tamsin’s funding inquiry. The encounter suggests a question about what an invitation to discuss a proposed opportunity communicates. It does not prove that actual applicants interpret it in either way. A staff member should distinguish a public inquiry, an application opportunity and an award notification, using the actual communication and contracting process. Listening must not become a private promise of funding or unauthorized information available to one prospective applicant.

You may reflect privately on how the book-exchange invitation changed your understanding. Agreement, a personal story, a live applicant meeting or a public work product is not required. The encounter cannot locate either person on an intercultural assessment continuum. Its value is learning to notice a plausible meaning, check it and revise communication with the other person’s actual perspective in view.

inThisLesson: Describe Mera’s and Dorian’s different learned meanings of an invitation.
Identify how an apparently welcoming phrase can imply a decision not yet made.
Revise the invitation so open influence and retained responsibility are clear.
Use the example for private understanding or a relevant inquiry.
lessons.keyStatement: Ask what the invitation means to its receiver before calling it clear or welcoming.

flashcards.back: For Mera, an invitation to bring a display recalls a place held for a guest. That personal meaning explains her preparation in the example, not a cultural rule for a group.
For Dorian, an invitation to discuss recalls ideas developed together before selection. That meaning does not automatically make the phrase clear to its receiver.
Explain what a participant can actually change. Asking for ideas after a choice is settled gives a different kind of participation from a genuinely open design inquiry.
Identify who still chooses the displays or makes the actual funding decision. Clarifying responsibility does not require dismissing another person’s interpretation.

items.title: Receive the interpretation
items.body: Mera’s account makes her preparation understandable without proving Dorian intended a promise. Check what was heard instead of deciding that one person was careless or that the phrase has one universal meaning.

items.title: Name the real opening
items.body: Dorian can state that display ideas may influence the plan while selection remains open. The clarification should correspond to the actual decision, not offer a polite invitation with no possible effect.

items.title: Carry the question carefully
items.body: In a funding inquiry, ask how a listener distinguishes discussion from commitment. Follow the applicable public communication and information rules. This example provides neither applicant evidence nor permission to give someone a private advantage.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretations and their implications

tabs.label: Insist the words were obvious
tabs.body: Repeating the phrase leaves Mera’s learned commitment meaning unexamined. Dorian’s intention explains only one side of the encounter; the receiver’s interpretation still affects preparation and expectations.

tabs.label: Promise a place to end tension
tabs.body: A promise might settle this conversation, but it would create a decision rather than clarify the earlier invitation. Dorian should not invent a selection merely to avoid acknowledging ambiguity.

tabs.label: Clarify influence and choice
tabs.body: Name what remains open, what Mera can influence and who retains selection. This can preserve meaningful exploration while making the invitation’s limits more understandable.

check.question: What is the most supported interpretation of the book-exchange misunderstanding?
check.correct: The supplied personal meanings differ: Mera hears a held place, while Dorian hears an open discussion; the invitation needs clarification.
wrong: Mera’s background means every member of her community expects a promise.
Dorian’s use of an open invitation proves an advanced assessment level.
The misunderstanding requires Dorian to reserve a display place.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The two original personal accounts explain the difference without creating a group rule or a selection.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One person’s supplied learning is not evidence about everyone in a community. A helpful intention or revision does not establish an intercultural assessment level. Clarifying an invitation does not require inventing a new commitment.

sorting.heading: Keep evidence, inquiry and decisions distinct

items.text: Mera associates the invitation with a held place.
Dorian associates discussion with shared exploration.
What part of the display plan can Mera influence?
Who still makes the display selection?
Every person from Mera’s community expects selection.
The encounter approves a DHS applicant.

lessons.next: Continue to compare evaluation choices with visible assumptions.

scenario.context: Practice book exchange: Mera starts preparing a display because she hears a held place. Dorian says selection is still open.
options: Explain what remains open and can be influenced, receive Mera’s interpretation and retain actual selection responsibility.
Describe Mera’s interpretation as a group habit.
Reserve a place solely to avoid discussing the meaning.
responses: This clarifies the actual invitation while preserving the receiver’s meaningful perspective.
The example describes an individual account, not evidence for a group profile.
A new promise avoids the interpretive question and creates an unsupported selection.

lessons.transfer: Privately explore how an invitation can be meaningful without being a promise. You can focus entirely on the example.

move.control: You can ask what an invitation communicates before judging a response.
move.failure: An open discussion is mistaken for a settled commitment.
move.next: Clarify real influence, retained responsibility and what the receiver heard.

lessons.title: Compare evaluation choices with visible assumptions
lessons.summary: Use a complete invented scoring comparison without treating practice weights as actual criteria or an award.
lessons.objective: Calculate two proposal totals from a complete invented rubric.
objectives: Calculate two proposal totals from a complete invented rubric.
Explain why a hypothetical weight change affects the comparison.
Distinguish a learning comparison from altering an actual published review.
takeaways: A total depends on the criteria, ratings and weights supplied.
Equal totals do not supply a tie-breaking or award rule.
Practice alternatives must not become quiet changes to actual criteria.
lessons.statement: Show how the comparison was built before interpreting what its total means.

image.caption: Two people review an open printed document, with one pointing to a line.

intro.heading: Compare evaluation choices with visible assumptions
intro.body:
For private arithmetic practice, Tamsin invents two proposals, Aster and Birch, and three criteria: described activity fit, described delivery preparation and described review approach. These labels and ratings are invented inputs, not findings about real organizations or an approved DHS rubric. The exercise rates each criterion from zero to four and assigns weights of forty, forty and twenty points. Each weighted result equals the rating divided by four, multiplied by its weight.

Aster’s supplied ratings are three, four and two. The weighted results are thirty, forty and ten, totaling eighty. Birch’s supplied ratings are four, two and four. Its results are forty, twenty and twenty, also totaling eighty. The tie is a complete practice calculation. The example describes no actual tie-breaking rule, threshold, available funding or recipient-selection authority. Neither proposal becomes an approved award.

Now examine a separate hypothetical design choice before any real posting: weights of twenty, sixty and twenty, with the invented ratings unchanged. Aster’s results become fifteen, sixty and ten, totaling eighty-five. Birch’s become twenty, thirty and twenty, totaling seventy. The difference changes because delivery preparation has more weight and activity fit less. It does not prove that Aster is more equitable, that Birch lacks ability or that the imagined weights should be adopted.

The exercise shows why criteria need a clear relationship to the purpose and appropriate review before use. A narrative may describe an activity, but the reader needs evidence for a rating and should distinguish writing presentation from what is actually being assessed. The supplied ratings let you calculate; they do not let you independently verify the underlying proposals.

In actual work, use the applicable published criteria and authorized review process. A preferred outcome does not justify privately changing a weight, softening a criterion for one applicant or inventing a tie rule. If a question emerges after posting, bring it to the responsible process with the relevant facts. You can learn from these two complete calculations without using a real application, revising a live solicitation or assigning a grant.

inThisLesson: Calculate two proposal totals from a complete invented rubric.
Explain why a hypothetical weight change affects the comparison.
Distinguish a learning comparison from altering an actual published review.
Use the example for private understanding or a relevant inquiry.
lessons.keyStatement: Show how the comparison was built before interpreting what its total means.

flashcards.back: In this invented exercise, divide a zero-to-four rating by four and multiply by the stated points. The formula describes this practice comparison only.
Both initial totals are eighty. The arithmetic does not supply a tie-breaking rule, eligible recipient, funding amount or authority to award.
The alternative weights make delivery preparation more influential. Changed totals show the effect of that assumption, not proof of an equitable design.
A supplied rating permits calculation but does not verify a proposal. In real review, the criterion, evidence and applicable process must support the judgment.

items.title: Calculate the initial comparison
items.body: Aster gives 3/4×40=30, 4/4×40=40 and 2/4×20=10. Birch gives 4/4×40=40, 2/4×40=20 and 4/4×20=20. Both total eighty; the calculation says nothing about an actual award.

items.title: Explain the alternative design
items.body: With twenty, sixty and twenty points, Aster totals fifteen plus sixty plus ten, or eighty-five. Birch totals twenty plus thirty plus twenty, or seventy. The same invented ratings interact with different weights.

items.title: Keep practice and actual review separate
items.body: A comparison can help examine what a proposed criterion emphasizes before authorized use. It cannot justify replacing actual published criteria, applying private exceptions or deciding a recipient outside the fitting process.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretations and their implications

tabs.label: Use the total as a verdict
tabs.body: An eighty-point tie says how the exercise inputs add up. It does not verify delivery, select a recipient or prove that the criteria examine the desired purpose fairly.

tabs.label: Change a weight to get the preferred winner
tabs.body: That approach works backward from a desired result and obscures the basis of review. The hypothetical design exercise must remain separate from any actual posted criteria.

tabs.label: Trace inputs and responsibility
tabs.body: Show the formula, ratings and weights, then identify the evidence and process still needed. The comparison becomes understandable without being inflated into an award recommendation.

check.question: What does the initial invented comparison show?
check.correct: Aster and Birch each total eighty under forty, forty and twenty weights; actual evidence, tie rules and award decisions are not supplied.
wrong: Aster totals ninety and is therefore selected.
Equal totals permit an arbitrary award to either organization.
The later eighty-five versus seventy comparison proves the alternative weights are equitable.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The two initial totals are eighty, and their limits remain visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Aster’s initial results are thirty, forty and ten, totaling eighty, not ninety. A numerical tie provides no actual tie-breaking or award authority. The alternative totals reflect changed assumptions, not verified equitable effects.

sorting.heading: Keep evidence, inquiry and decisions distinct

items.text: Aster totals eighty with forty, forty and twenty weights.
Birch totals eighty with forty, forty and twenty weights.
Aster totals eighty-five with twenty, sixty and twenty weights.
Birch totals seventy with twenty, sixty and twenty weights.
An eighty-point tie creates an actual award rule.
A preferred result permits quiet changes to posted weights.

lessons.next: Continue to keep a review question with its actual responsibility.

scenario.context: Practice: Tamsin sees that changed weights favor Aster and suggests using them after actual proposals have been received. No authorized process is supplied.
options: Apply the changed weights only to Aster.
Keep the exercise comparison separate and bring any actual review question to the responsible process.
Treat the original tie as permission to award arbitrarily.
responses: Different private criteria would obscure the basis of the actual review and create an unsupported advantage.
This preserves useful learning while retaining the actual criteria and review responsibility.
A practice tie creates neither recipient-selection authority nor an actual tie rule.

lessons.transfer: Privately check the two sets of invented totals and identify which changed assumption explains the difference.

move.control: You can make a calculation and its assumptions visible.
move.failure: A practice comparison becomes an unauthorized change or recipient decision.
move.next: Retain the stated inputs and distinguish design inquiry from actual review.

lessons.title: Keep a review question with its actual responsibility
lessons.summary: Distinguish useful design discussion from a disclosed conflict or a contracting decision that needs its real process.
lessons.objective: Identify the actual conflict-review question raised by Oren’s practice connection.
objectives: Identify the actual conflict-review question raised by Oren’s practice connection.
Distinguish disclosure from a finding or resolution of the conflict.
Describe a suitable process inquiry without inventing posting or scoring authority.
takeaways: Disclosing a relationship is not the same as resolving it.
A learning discussion cannot replace actual conflict and contracting processes.
Clear responsibility makes useful inquiry possible without an improvised decision.
lessons.statement: Name the question, provide the relevant facts and preserve the responsible decision process.

image.caption: Two people review an open printed document, with one pointing to a line.

intro.heading: Keep a review question with its actual responsibility
intro.body:
In an original practice competitive-grant review, Oren is a state employee scoring applications and has volunteered with an applicant organization. Oren tells Tamsin about the connection before reviewing that application. The case gives a relationship that needs the applicable conflict process. It does not establish that Oren is dishonest, that a prohibited act occurred or that the connection has been resolved. A statement that Oren will “try to be fair” would not examine those questions.

The current Office of Grants Management conflict policy requires the competitive-review disclosure form and a fitting process for an actual or potential conflict. For a state employee scoring applications, identification calls for immediate action through the appropriate agency or grant-program personnel. Volunteer connections are examined case by case. Tamsin should use that actual process rather than declare every volunteer connection harmless or automatically disqualifying. If the ordinary responsible contact is involved, the policy’s alternate route matters; learning must not send the question back only to that person.

Separate disclosure from resolution. A signed form records information; the actual process examines the relationship and appropriate steps. The exercise gives no resolution or permission for Oren to continue that application’s review. It also gives no reason to declare every unrelated panel member or activity stopped. Which actions can proceed needs the relevant facts and responsible guidance, not a course-created blanket rule.

Tamsin also asks whether the proposed instruction format may change and whether an inherited insurance clause is appropriate. Those are different questions. Staff can prepare the task evidence and a proposed alternative, but actual solicitation and contract review must follow DHS’s applicable contracting process, including relevant exceptions. Neither consultant program leadership nor a panel discussion creates posting, execution or exception authority.

For private learning, identify which fact Oren should disclose and which decision the example does not show. You do not need to upload a real disclosure, name an actual applicant or publish an account of your relationships. In real work, use the required formal records and responsible routes. The course can strengthen understanding without deciding the conflict or standing in for required grants-management training.

inThisLesson: Identify the actual conflict-review question raised by Oren’s practice connection.
Distinguish disclosure from a finding or resolution of the conflict.
Describe a suitable process inquiry without inventing posting or scoring authority.
Use the example for private understanding or a relevant inquiry.
lessons.keyStatement: Name the question, provide the relevant facts and preserve the responsible decision process.

flashcards.back: Oren’s volunteer connection raises an actual-process question. It does not itself prove misconduct, harmlessness or a resolved conflict.
The actual competitive-review form and relevant facts support the responsible process. A disclosure is distinct from a decision about how to address the relationship.
The fitting agency process determines appropriate steps from the facts. The course does not authorize continued review, blanket exclusion or a new decision rule.
Staff can prepare a proposed change and its rationale. Actual posting, contract review and exceptions retain the applicable DHS process and delegated responsibilities.

items.title: Do not delay the actual route
items.body: Oren’s promise of impartiality does not resolve the identified question. Use the fitting disclosure and personnel route promptly; for a state employee scoring applications the policy requires immediate action upon identification.

items.title: Keep the fact and decision separate
items.body: The relationship, its scope and any relevant context inform the process. A label such as volunteer does not by itself establish either a safe connection or an automatic bar. The actual resolution must remain visible.

items.title: Prepare a useful separate proposal
items.body: The instruction-format and insurance questions can be described with their purpose, task evidence and open conditions. The relevant contracting review still decides what can be posted or executed; do not turn a learning suggestion into approval.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretations and their implications

tabs.label: Rely on a promise
tabs.body: Oren may sincerely intend fairness, but an assurance does not complete the actual conflict process. The application review question needs the required disclosure and responsible examination.

tabs.label: Invent a blanket outcome
tabs.body: Declaring that every volunteer is excluded or all work must stop bypasses the case-specific process. The example supplies neither the necessary facts nor an actual resolution.

tabs.label: Use the fitting process
tabs.body: Retain Oren’s connection, use the actual disclosure and appropriate personnel route, and obtain the real resolution. Keep separate contracting questions in their own applicable review rather than combine everything into a panel judgment.

check.question: How should Tamsin treat Oren’s volunteered connection?
check.correct: Use the actual disclosure and appropriate personnel process without treating the connection as either harmless, misconduct or already resolved.
wrong: A promise of fairness is enough to close the question.
Every volunteer connection automatically bars a person from scoring.
A completed course permits Oren to review the application.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The relationship needs its actual process; the exercise does not supply a resolution.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An assurance of intent does not complete the required disclosure and conflict process. The actual policy calls for case-specific examination of volunteer connections. Course completion establishes no conflict resolution or review permission.

lessons.summary: Repair an overstatement, retain useful improvements and identify what the imagined planning work still does not show.

lessons.statement: Say what was actually improved without turning a planning repair into a service outcome.

intro.heading: Correct the account and keep later effects open
intro.body:
Tamsin drafts a closing sentence: “The course has approved an equitable grant and ensured that new organizations can deliver the service.” Galen checks it against the example. The work has clarified an intended information-access purpose, identified an image-only instructional barrier, examined an invitation’s meaning and compared invented rubric choices. No actual funding arrangement, posting, award, eligible recipient or service delivery has been supplied. The closing sentence overstates both authority and effects.

They revise the account. The draft now separates the purpose from the open contracting questions. A proposed structured instruction version preserves the need to check the actual authoritative requirements. A proposed inquiry distinguishes discussion from an award commitment. The invented calculations remain clearly marked as learning comparisons. Oren’s disclosed relationship retains its actual conflict process and an open resolution. These are particular improvements in the explanation; they do not complete a solicitation.

An honest next inquiry follows the missing link. Has the fitting process established which arrangement applies? Can the intended reader use the revised instruction task? What does a potential participant understand to be open or promised? Which evidence supports the actual criteria? How was an identified conflict addressed? These questions should be asked within the real responsibility, information and communication arrangements rather than create a new collection of private applicant records in a course.

The DHS Equity Policy includes RFP, contracting and procurement work. Where an action meets its formal-review conditions, use the required analysis or scan, or a relevant customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director. A learning checklist does not certify that requirement. Required grants-management training still applies. The appropriate formal process remains necessary even when a learner has completed every activity.

You can close privately by correcting one practice claim and identifying one later question. No live solicitation, new application target or public work product is required. Better understanding has value before an operational change is made. If the practice later informs your actual work, retain the difference between a proposed improvement, its authorized use and a meaningful effect for the people the program intends to serve.

lessons.keyStatement: Say what was actually improved without turning a planning repair into a service outcome.

flashcards.back: The draft more accurately describes purpose, proposed format and open decisions. That is progress in the account, not a completed solicitation or award.
A reader’s ability to use the task, opportunity awareness and actual service effects are distinct questions. One repaired paragraph does not answer all of them.
Qualifying actions retain the actual DHS analysis or scan requirement, or relevant customized-tool route. Completing this learning does not certify formal compliance.
Correcting a claim can strengthen understanding without a live posting or public product. Actual professional duties and required training still follow their fitting processes.

items.title: Remove the authority overclaim
items.body: Nothing in the example approves a grant or awards funding. Keep the intended purpose and the useful proposals, while identifying the actual contracting and decision questions that remain.

items.title: Remove the effect overclaim
items.body: A proposed readable version addresses a task barrier; it does not show new applicants, successful delivery or equitable service results. Identify the fitting later evidence instead of predicting those effects as facts.

items.title: Preserve the required work
items.body: Formal equity, conflict, contracting and training requirements retain their actual conditions. A learning checklist supports inquiry but cannot substitute for the applicable decisions, records or authorized process.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretations and their implications

tabs.label: Announce complete success
tabs.body: That conclusion makes proposed clarity stand for approval, participation and services. It hides precisely the unanswered links the course helped identify.

tabs.label: Dismiss the work as nothing
tabs.body: An open decision does not make the clarified purpose and corrected claims worthless. Particular learning and planning improvements can matter without pretending to be a completed outcome.

tabs.label: Describe progress and remaining questions
tabs.body: State the specific revision and the later task, process and effect questions. This gives a useful account that can guide further work without making unsupported promises.

check.question: Which closing account matches the practice work?
check.correct: The draft clarifies the purpose and proposed improvements; actual arrangement, posting, conflict resolution, participation and service effects remain open.
wrong: Every future applicant will now succeed.
The course certifies formal equity and contracting compliance.
No useful learning occurred because no award was made.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The particular improvements and their limits are both retained.
check.feedbackIncorrect: No future applicant result is supplied, and a format proposal cannot guarantee success. Completion does not establish actual formal review, approval or conflict resolution. Private understanding and a corrected explanation have value before an operational outcome.

items.text: The draft separates a proposed purpose from approval.
The practice weights and their totals are visible.
Can the actual reader use the revised instructions?
How was Oren’s relationship actually resolved?

lessons.next: Use the job aid for private reflection or a relevant inquiry within your actual responsibility.

scenario.context: Practice close: Tamsin wants to call the repaired draft a successful service-access intervention. No actual use or service evidence is supplied.
options: Keep the particular drafting improvements and name the real process and evidence questions still open.
Claim wider service access because the document looks clearer.
Discard the learning because no live award occurred.
responses: This retains useful progress while avoiding an approval or effect claim the case cannot support.
Visual clarity alone does not establish actual use, awards or service access.
A clearer distinction and private learning can be valuable without a live outcome.

lessons.transfer: Privately rewrite the practice closing sentence and choose one proportionate evidence question for later inquiry.

move.control: You can describe a useful revision and its practical limits.
move.failure: Planning clarity becomes a claim of approval or equitable results.
move.next: Retain the specific improvement and the next actual-process or evidence question.

jobAid.title: Examine an opportunity without inventing an award
jobAid.subtitle: Clarify purpose, trace actual tasks and preserve the fitting process and evidence.
remember: A proposed purpose is not an approved opportunity.
A task barrier is not an organization’s capacity profile.
A disclosed relationship is not a resolved conflict, and a practice total is not an award.

sections.heading: Clarify purpose and arrangement
items: Describe the intended purpose, what is proposed and what the case actually supplies. Tamsin’s information-learning idea supplies no appropriation, amount, eligible organization, funding condition or decision authority.
Distinguish a grant supporting a legally authorized public purpose from a procurement purchase using the actual contracting responsibility. Do not let a familiar template make that determination.
Keep a planning inquiry separate from actual posting, recipient selection, an agreement or permission to spend. Staff can prepare evidence and proposals without inventing delegated powers.

sections.heading: Trace task barriers and participation
items: Keep Ellis’s image-only reading-software report attached to the instructional task. The example describes no diagnosis, organization size, eligibility or delivery-capacity conclusion.
Propose structured, usable instructions that preserve the actual authoritative conditions. A summary or format repair cannot quietly waive eligibility, financial or service obligations.
A familiar-only response pool does not show who saw the notice or why others declined. Examine competing explanations and the evidence needed rather than invent a distribution or capacity cause.
Use the actual review and communication route for changes to a posted document or process. A clearer draft does not certify universal access or create successful new applicants.

sections.heading: Receive meanings and show assumptions
items: Mera learned an invitation as a held-place commitment; Dorian learned discussion as shared exploration. Clarify what remains open, what can actually be influenced and who retains selection. These are meanings the people describe, not a group profile or development assessment.

A public inquiry, application opportunity and award notification communicate different commitments. Preserve actual communication and information requirements; the encounter permits no private funding promise or unauthorized applicant advantage.

Complete initial practice rubric: zero-to-four ratings divided by four and multiplied by forty, forty and twenty points. Aster 3/4/2 gives 30+40+10=80; Birch 4/2/4 gives 40+20+20=80. No actual tie rule, funding or selection is supplied.

Complete alternative practice weights 20/60/20 with unchanged ratings: Aster 15+60+10=85; Birch 20+30+20=70. Changed totals show a changed assumption, not equitable effects or verified proposal quality.
Keep the practice design comparison separate from actual published criteria and review. Do not use preferred results to quietly change weights, soften a criterion or invent award authority.

sections.heading: Use the actual responsibility
items: Oren is a state employee scoring applications, so the volunteer connection requires the actual competitive-review disclosure and appropriate personnel process. The policy’s immediate action and alternate route remain applicable; volunteer connections are examined case by case.

Keep the connection, disclosure and resolution distinct. An impartiality promise, signed form or course completion does not alone resolve the relationship or permit continued review. The actual process must determine appropriate steps.

Describe the format or inherited-clause question for the applicable DHS contracting review, including relevant exceptions. Consultant leadership, a panel discussion and an intended benefit do not create posting, execution or exception authority.

Where an action meets DHS Equity Policy formal-review conditions, retain the required analysis or scan, or relevant customized-tool route developed in consultation with an equity director. A course checklist cannot certify compliance.

sections.heading: Close with honest progress
items: Replace Tamsin’s approval and service-success overclaim with the particular purpose, draft and comparison improvements. Actual arrangement, posting, award, conflict resolution, use and effects remain open.

Choose a proportionate later task or evidence inquiry within actual information and communication processes. Do not build a private applicant-history collection in a course or treat unknown participation as zero.
Private learning and a corrected interpretation are valuable without a live opportunity or public product. Actual duties and required grants-management training remain separate.
Native American- and Tribal-specific matters go to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
